definitions.explanation: Expresses movement toward the speaker's current location or reference point. The opposite of {行|い}く (to go). Used when the speaker is at or identifies with the destination.
When attached to the te-form of another verb (〜てくる), indicates an action that has been continuing up to the present, or movement toward the speaker.

examples.japanese: {友達|ともだち}が{家|いえ}に{来|き}ました。
examples.english: My friend came to my house.

examples.japanese: {毎週|まいしゅう}{日曜日|にちようび}に{友達|ともだち}が{遊|あそ}びに{来|く}る。
examples.english: Every Sunday my friend comes over to hang out.

examples.japanese: バスがなかなか{来|こ}なくて、{三十|さんじゅっ}{分|ぷん}も{待|ま}った。
examples.english: The bus wasn't coming, so I waited for thirty minutes.

examples.notes: 〜てくる expressing beginning of an action

examples.japanese: {日本語|にほんご}が{分|わ}かるようになってきた。
{走|はし}っていたら、{暑|あつ}くなってきた。
examples.english: While I was running, I started to get hot.

examples.japanese: ずっと{練習|れんしゅう}してきたので、{今|いま}は{上手|じょうず}に{話|はな}せるようになった。
examples.english: Because I've been practicing all along, I can now speak well.
examples.notes: 〜てくる expressing action continuing up to the present

notes:
TRANSITIVITY: {自動詞|じどうし} (intransitive). Counterpart: {行|い}く (to go). Pattern: Xに/へ{来|く}る (come to X).

ASPECT: ている indicates resulting state or habitual. {来|き}ている = 'has come (and is here)' or 'comes regularly.'

COMMON PATTERNS:
・{家|いえ}に{来|く}る (come to the house)
・{遊|あそ}びに{来|く}る (come to hang out)
・〜て{来|く}る (come after doing ~, or change up to now)
・{来|く}るようになる (come to do something regularly)

IRREGULAR VERB: One of only two irregular verbs (with する). Reading changes: く→こ (negative), く→き (te-form, past, polite).
